overview.summary: A Trie (pronounced 'try') is a specialized tree used to store associative data structures, specifically strings. It excels at fast prefix matching.
learningObjectives: Recognize autocomplete and spell-check as Trie use cases.
overview.interviewRelevance: Tries appear whenever an interview asks you to build 'Autocomplete', 'Search History', or 'Dictionary Spell Check'. It's the ultimate string-search data structure.

paragraphs: When you type 'algo' into Google, how does it instantly suggest 'algorithm', 'algorand', and 'algodones'?
It doesn't scan millions of words starting with A, then L, then G. It follows a path down a Trie: A -> L -> G -> O, and simply returns all the leaves below that exact node.
realWorldHook.ahaMoment: In a Trie, the data is not stored IN the nodes. The data is defined by the PATH you take to get there.

definition.technicalDefinition: A Trie is a tree-like data structure whose nodes store the letters of an alphabet. By structuring the nodes in a particular way, words and strings can be retrieved by traversing down a branch path of the tree.

vocabulary.definition: The beginning characters of a word.
A boolean stored on a node to indicate that the path ending at this node forms a complete valid word.
Instead of just Left/Right, a Trie node has a Hash Map (or Array of size 26) pointing to its children.

keyProperties: O(L) search time, where L is the length of the word (independent of how many words are in the dictionary).
Extremely memory efficient for storing words with shared prefixes.

metaphor: A file cabinet with folders inside of folders. The top drawer is 'A', inside is 'P', inside is 'P', inside is 'L', inside is 'E'.
mentalModel.clickSentence: By sharing common prefixes, the words 'cat', 'car', and 'cap' all share the exact same 'c -> a' nodes in memory.

memoryDescription: A TrieNode has two things: A Hash Map (or Array[26]) of children, and a boolean flag `is_word`.
The letter itself isn't technically stored in the node; it is the KEY in the parent's Hash Map that points to the child.

operations.name: Insert
operations.description: Walk down the tree creating new nodes for characters that don't exist yet. Mark the final node with is_word = True.
operations.visualNote: A path lights up, spawning new nodes when needed.

operations.name: Search / StartsWith
operations.description: Walk down the tree following the characters. If a character is missing, return false.
operations.visualNote: A pointer traces down the existing letters.

patternTemplate.whenToUse: Whenever a problem asks you to search for words, prefixes, or do autocomplete across a massive dictionary of strings.
patternTemplate.timeComplexity: O(L) where L is string length.

recognitionQuiz.problemStatement: Design a data structure that supports adding new words and finding if a string matches any previously added string, where the string can contain the '.' wildcard character.
recognitionQuiz.explanation: Because of the '.' wildcard (which can match ANY letter), a Hash Map fails. A Trie allows you to run a DFS down every child branch when you hit a wildcard.

examples.title: Implement Trie (Prefix Tree)
examples.problemStatement: Implement the Trie class with insert, search, and startsWith methods.
examples.inputExample: Trie trie = new Trie(); trie.insert("apple"); trie.search("apple");
steps: Implement Insert by iterating chars and building nodes.
Implement Search by iterating chars and returning the final isWord flag.
Implement StartsWith the same way, but return true immediately if you reach the end of the prefix.
examples.rationale: This perfectly encapsulates the core operations of the data structure without external logic.

conceptQuiz.question: If you insert 'cat' and 'car' into an empty Trie, how many nodes (including root) exist?
options: 6 nodes (Root, c, a, t, c, a, r)

conceptQuiz.question: Why use a Trie over a Hash Map for dictionary lookups?
options: A Trie can instantly find all words that START WITH a specific prefix, which a Hash Map cannot do.
A Trie uses less CPU cycles.
conceptQuiz.explanation: A Hash Map only supports exact matches. To find prefixes in a Hash Map, you would have to iterate over every single key in the map (O(N)).

practice.title: Design Add and Search Words Data Structure
practice.keyInsight: When you hit a '.' wildcard, run a DFS on all children of the current node.

practice.title: Word Search II
practice.keyInsight: Put the dictionary into a Trie, then run DFS from every cell on the board, walking down the Trie concurrently.
